title: The Docks of New York
byline: Dir. Josef von Sternberg. Paramount Pictures, 1928. Silent. Screenplay by Jules Furthman from John Monk Saunders's story 'The Dock Walloper.' Stars George Bancroft, Betty Compson.

editorial:
Josef von Sternberg's final silent feature for Paramount stars George Bancroft as Bill Roberts, a coal stoker on a harbor barge who hauls Mae (Betty Compson) out of the Hudson River after she tries to drown herself, then impulsively marries her before the next tide carries him away. Cinematographer Harold Rosson packed every frame with harbor smoke, gaslight, and cramped waterfront interiors â€” a nocturnal world of dockworkers, transient sailors, and women with nowhere else to go. Jules Furthman adapted John Monk Saunders's original story 'The Dock Walloper'; the film premiered in New York on September 16, 1928, and the Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 1999 as culturally and aesthetically significant.

The 1928 Paramount print entered US public domain on January 1, 2024, when its 95-year copyright term expired, and the silent picture itself is freely reusable â€” the original release had no recorded soundtrack to complicate the picture track. The one live trap is sourcing from commercial restorations: the Criterion Collection edition (spine #531, 'Three Silent Classics by Josef von Sternberg') and Kino Lorber releases each pair a new digital restoration with a newly composed or arranged score, and both elements carry their own copyrights entirely separate from the underlying 1928 film. A creator who rips from those discs is not using the public-domain original â€” they are copying protected restoration work. The clean path is the unadorned archive.org uploads, which circulate the silent print without a modern recorded score attached.
faq: Is the film itself free to use?

Yes. Paramount published The Docks of New York in September 1928, and its 95-year US copyright term expired on January 1, 2024. The original silent print is in the public domain and requires no license.
What about the score on the Criterion or Kino Lorber release?

The original film was silent; any music heard on a commercial disc is a newly composed or arranged work protected under its own copyright, entirely separate from the PD print. To stay unencumbered, source from an archive.org copy that carries no modern recorded score â€” do not rip from a Criterion or Kino disc.
